video_title: Ethereum’s New EIP Could Break DeFi
gist: Bankless host David hosts Stonnie (Aave) and Mike (EtherFi) to attack a new Ethereum 'stake targeting / stake tapering' EIP from six Ethereum Foundation researchers that would drive staking issuance toward zero as staked ETH approaches ~50% (currently ~34% staked). The guests argue it kills solo-staker economics at a ~2% reserve yield, centralizes staking into zero-cost-of-capital exchanges and DATs plus one dominant LST, triggers a capital exodus from seven of the top ten DeFi protocols, and turns ETH into a yen-style carry-trade funding leg that rotates capital into stablecoins and competing chains. Both hosts and guests also flag the process legitimacy problem: the EIP landed days before the hard-fork inclusion meeting, and the host closes predicting it will not pass.

insights.claim: Six Ethereum Foundation researchers and developers proposed a 'stake targeting / stake tapering' EIP because there is currently no cap on the incentive to stake ETH — roughly 34% of all ETH is staked today and the proposers fear it marches toward 100%, with vanilla ETH progressively replaced by staked-ETH derivatives from Lido, Rocketpool and EtherFi.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: A live protocol-level change to ETH monetary policy is the single biggest swing factor for LST issuers and ETH staking-yield-linked assets; watch the hard-fork inclusion process.
insights.quote: Right now there is about 34% of all ETH is staked and the worry that this EIP has is that that will slowly march increasingly close to 100% because there's no reason for it not to.

insights.claim: The EIP's mechanic is a taper in which staking yield approaches zero as staked ETH approaches a 50% target, burning the issuance above that point rather than paying it to validators.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: Any model of ETH staking revenue, LST fee income or DAT cash flows must stress-test a scenario where the marginal staking yield asymptotes to zero above a 50% stake ratio.
insights.quote: essentially yield approaches zero as staked teeth approaches 50%

insights.claim: The proposers' security argument is that Ethereum is overpaying for security and that roughly 30–40% of ETH staked already provides ample security, so no more than 50% is needed.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: The whole EIP rests on an unproven 'sufficient security' threshold; if that assumption is contested successfully, the proposal loses its core justification.
insights.quote: something around 30 to 40% of ETH staked to Ethereum provides ample security according to the opinions of these researchers

insights.claim: The EIP was introduced only days before the All Core Devs meeting where proposals were considered for inclusion in the next hard fork, creating the impression it was being squeezed in without debate — which backfired and produced near-universal opposition outside the EF.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: Process optics, not economics, may be what kills this EIP — a template for how contentious Ethereum monetary changes get defeated.
insights.quote: it was proposed with you know a matter of days uh leading up to the meeting where where these proposals were discussed for inclusion and in the next hard fork

themes.theme: Solo Staker Economics and Validator Centralization

insights.claim: Solo stakers have the highest cost basis on Ethereum because they get no economies of scale, and at current costs a 2% to 2.5% yield is roughly break-even, so any issuance cut pushes every solo staker into a loss.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: The floor under Ethereum's decentralized validator set is a hard cost number, not ideology — issuance cuts translate mechanically into node shutdowns.
insights.quote: a two and a half% yield, 2% yield is is pretty much break even at this point um in terms of the cost of operating a note

insights.claim: An ETHStaker survey found the reserve price for most solo stakers is 2% — below that yield they say they will turn off their nodes — making the belief that thousands of operators will keep running at a loss 'magical thinking'.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: 2% staking yield is the empirically stated cliff for solo-staker attrition; it is the level to watch for validator-set decentralization metrics.
insights.quote: there was a survey fairly recently by done by ETH staker uh that showed that the sort of reserve price uh for most solar stakers is 2%

insights.claim: Because exchanges and treasury companies like Coinbase, Binance, Sharplink and Bitmine have effectively no cost of capital on user-deposited or balance-sheet ETH, they would keep staking even at 20 basis points, so the taper causes an exodus of independent operators and centralizes the network in exactly the entities it claims to protect against.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: Post-taper, staking market share would concentrate in listed custodians and DATs — bullish their staking-share narrative, bearish Ethereum's decentralization story.
insights.quote: this is going to centralize the network because entities like Coinbase and Binance and Sharlink and you know Bitmine they have no cost of capital right

insights.claim: At 20 to 50 basis points of staking yield an LST issuer earns only about one basis point of revenue, so liquid staking would immediately consolidate into a single giant LST because only massive scale could fund developers and audits.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: The taper is a winner-take-all forcing function in liquid staking — smaller LST tokens would be structurally impaired while the largest incumbent consolidates share.
insights.quote: LSTs will immediately concentrate into one giant LST, liquid staking tokens, because at 20 basis points, 50 basis points, you're only making one basis point of of revenue

insights.claim: Beyond lower cash flows, the tapering design creates unpredictable tax consequences for solo stakers, who could receive a tax bill on staking income large enough to push their net position negative.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Tax drag on a variable, tapering yield is a second-order reason retail staking participation would fall faster than the raw yield math implies.
insights.quote: creates also uh very unpredictable tax consequences. So you know and the question is then if someone gets a $500 bill for staking uh they can even go into negative as well

insights.claim: If the stake tapering EIP passes, seven of the top ten DeFi protocols would face a massive capital exodus as the ETH-denominated base yield they are built on disappears.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: The concentration of DeFi TVL in staking-yield-dependent strategies means the largest ETH DeFi tokens would be the direct casualties of this EIP.
insights.quote: the seven of the top 10 DeFi protocols would face a massive capital exodus

insights.claim: Staking yield functions as Ethereum's foundational yield layer the way short-term T-bills do in traditional finance, with roughly a hundred layers of derivatives stacked on top — so changing the issuance curve is analogous to the US government tapering T-bill rates when too many people buy them.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for pricing protocol-level yield changes: the risk is not the base rate itself but the leveraged stack built on its predictability.
insights.quote: if you're messing with this foundational yield layer on top of which a lot of other things are stacked I mean you're going to you're going to really break the system

insights.claim: Most DeFi yield on Ethereum ultimately derives from native staking routed through liquid staking derivatives, which create the borrowing demand in lending protocols by letting users enter and exit staking without going through the validator queue — so 'go find yield in DeFi instead' is circular reasoning.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Lending-protocol borrow demand and looping strategies are downstream of staking yield; a taper compresses lending revenue across the sector, not just LST fees.
insights.quote: a lot of the yield actually comes from these u uh uh liquid staking um uh derivatives that basically just makes it more feasible to stake and come in and out and then that creates the the borrowing demand

insights.claim: Removing the staking base yield forces ETH holders further up the risk curve because there is no other scalable, low-risk source of ETH-denominated yield outside native staking.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Post-taper, ETH yield products would have to take real credit or duration risk, raising systemic fragility in DeFi rather than reducing it.
insights.quote: I don't particularly know many yield sources at a scalable way where you can actually get yield on ETH beyond the sort of like a uh kind of like a risk-free or this low uh risk um yield that is derived from uh native uh uh staking

insights.claim: Mike argues liquid staking tokens deliver application-layer user protections that would be inappropriate at the network level — for example governance-approved forks to rescue funds after a North Korean exploit — for only five to ten basis points, and that the better fix for the EF's concerns is to enshrine LSTs in the protocol rather than alter the issuance curve.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: An enshrined-LST design is the concrete alternative on the table; it would disintermediate Lido and EtherFi's staking business while preserving DeFi's yield base.
insights.quote: My perspective is and I've argued this in the past is that we should just enshrine LSTs and that that kicks

themes.theme: Nominal vs Real Yield and the Fixed-Supply Argument

insights.claim: Mike argues a fixed money supply is bad economics for a real economy — citing Milton Friedman's prescription of a fixed 3% annual money-supply growth — and calls the push toward zero ETH issuance a 'bitcoin brainworm' because deflation is in some ways worse than inflation.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: The strongest intellectual counter to ultrasound-money framing: a deflationary ETH becomes hard to use as debt collateral or money, capping Ethereum's economic ambitions.
insights.quote: this argument that we need to have zero issuance in some at some point is a really bad argument that it's like a bitcoin brainworm

insights.claim: Mike contends the case is stronger that ETH staking yield should be higher, not lower, since even at 100% staked and zero burn the inflation is about 1.5% — and with EIP1559 burn it is lower — a trivial problem relative to breaking the yield layer.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: Frames the whole debate as optimizing away ~1.5% of dilution at the cost of the ecosystem's core yield infrastructure — a poor risk/reward for ETH holders.
insights.quote: let's say burn goes to zero 100% of ETH is staked how much of a problem is 1.5% % yield. I think the case is actually stronger that the yield should be higher than that it should be lower.

insights.claim: Because in traditional markets the derivatives market is more than ten times the size of the spot market, Mike argues that if Ethereum becomes the platform for all of finance essentially all ETH will end up in derivatives regardless of issuance policy, making the EIP's 'preserve vanilla ETH' goal a red herring.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: If derivatization is inevitable, the investable layer is the issuers of ETH derivatives and their fee capture, not vanilla ETH holding.
insights.quote: If you look at the trady markets the market for derivatives is 10 times more more than 10 times the size of the market for spot.

insights.claim: The host's steelman is that ETH staking yield is purely nominal — newly minted ETH paid to stakers — while real yield is only transaction fees and burn, so tapering removes a fake game and lets users hold vanilla, intermediary-free ETH without being inflated away.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: The nominal-vs-real-yield distinction is the cleanest bull case for the EIP and the argument LST holders must be able to rebut.
insights.quote: the ETH stake rate is a nominal yield because we are minting ETH as we are giving it to the ETH to the ETH stakers. Real yield is not happening. Real yield is the transaction fees that are paid to stakers

insights.claim: Mike's rebuttal is that staking de facto serves two different functions — paying for network security and providing an economy's savings rate — and that if the economy grows faster than issuance, stakers earn genuine real yield; conflating the two is what generates the confusion behind the EIP.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: Separating 'security budget' from 'savings rate' is the analytical frame for judging any future Ethereum issuance proposal.
insights.quote: staking uh is de facto serving these two purposes that on the one hand it's providing security to the Ethereum network and there's lots of complications around that and then on the other hand it also provides this again de facto benefit

themes.theme: ETH as Funding Leg and Rotation into Stablecoins

insights.claim: Stonnie argues that stripping ETH of its yield turns it into a funding leg like the Japanese yen in the world's largest carry trade — borrowed cheaply and sold to buy a productive asset — creating structural sell pressure on ETH, the opposite of the proposal's stated goal of making ETH better money.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: A zero-yield ETH would likely see rising borrow demand paired with spot selling — a bearish flow dynamic to watch in on-chain lending markets.
insights.quote: And if there's no yield on uh on it on DeFi, what it means is that um it as an asset becomes a funding leg

insights.claim: Stonnie predicts stablecoins are the biggest winners from an ETH yield taper, as holders who want cash flow rotate out of ETH positions into on-chain stablecoin yields, mirroring how low rates in traditional finance push money between risk assets and cash.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Trade expression: long stablecoin-yield infrastructure and short ETH-denominated yield products if the EIP gains traction.
insights.quote: Um and I think there uh the biggest the biggest winners are actually stable coins

insights.claim: Stonnie warns that value leaving ETH would go not only to stablecoins but to competing networks such as Solana, which he calls the worst possible outcome for Ethereum and a return to the earliest, most competitive phase of the blockchain story.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Frames the EIP as a relative-value risk for ETH versus competing L1s, not just an internal Ethereum design question.
insights.quote: otherwise if that doesn't exist all that value goes into stable coins um and also competing uh networks and that is the worst outcome for Ethereum

insights.claim: David argues killing staking yield would be devastating for Tom Lee, who deployed roughly $10 billion into ETH and uses the staking yield as his primary tool for selling ETH to other institutions — and worse for every future institutional buyer who would have copied him.
insights.speaker: David (Bankless host)
insights.so_what: ETH treasury companies are the marginal institutional bid; a yield taper directly undermines their pitch and mNAV narrative.
insights.quote: imagine what that message would be like if like one year after Tom Lee buys $10 billion of ETH, the ETH protocol kills yield and now he doesn't get any yield

insights.claim: Stonnie says staking yield is what lets ETH treasury companies underwrite ETH as a cash-flow asset, and without it they would be forced into 'ponzenomics' of the kind MicroStrategy runs to sustain their premium.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Distinguishes ETH DATs from BTC DATs on the basis of a real cash-flow claim; removing yield collapses that differentiation.
insights.quote: if they don't have any yield they will have to do you know ponzenomics like what micro strategy is doing

insights.claim: Stonnie cites a Joseph Chalom post from Sharplink to argue the timing is uniquely bad because Ethereum is in the 'last mile' of asset distribution — ETFs, institutional adoption, and a CLARITY Act that would let every US bank launch crypto custody and lending businesses without pre-approval — with ETH's savings rate being the feature that positions it ahead of Bitcoin and Solana.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: If the CLARITY Act passes, bank distribution of ETH would hinge on its yield; a taper would remove ETH's key differentiator right as that channel opens.
insights.quote: if clarity act passes obviously what it means that every single bank uh in in in in US can actually set up uh crypto-based businesses without any sort of a pre-approval

insights.claim: Mike argues the perception that this change was jammed through governance destroys Ethereum's credibility with nation states and large institutions — El Salvador chose Bitcoin precisely because it is ossified and predictable — and that this episode creates zero chance a nation state builds on Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Mike (EtherFi)
insights.so_what: Reframes monetary-policy tinkering as a direct hit to Ethereum's credibly-neutral moat versus Bitcoin — a long-horizon adoption risk, not a short-term yield question.
insights.quote: This kind of thing I think creates a zero chance that they choose Ethereum

insights.claim: Stonnie says the biggest fear in the community is not the EIP itself but that the Ethereum Foundation's researchers are disconnected from DeFi builders and will not listen to concrete feedback, repeating a pattern from earlier proposals that drew backlash.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: Governance-process risk is now an input into ETH's institutional narrative; watch whether the EF withdraws or modifies the EIP after feedback.
insights.quote: the the big concern amongst the the the developers particularly is the uh the disconnection between the um EF uh sort of uh researchers um developers from like the the rest of the ecosystem and DeFi

insights.claim: Stonnie argues Ethereum's real problem is demand-side and product completeness — it still lacks good privacy and good scalability while security is its one finished component — so the ecosystem should stop playing issuance games instead of axing the one thing that works.
insights.speaker: Stonnie (Aave)
insights.so_what: A roadmap-priority signal: privacy and scaling deliverables, not monetary tweaks, are what this cohort of builders believes will re-rate ETH.
insights.quote: We shouldn't be focusing on optimizing issuance. We we should be focusing on how do we make Ethereum like a better product.
